title: Welcome
text: This guide explains how to use your company's operations platform: the one place for work orders, purchasing, quality, safety, people matters, books and reports. It is written for the people who use it every day, not for programmers. Where something is only for the person who sets the system up, you will see a short box that points to the Administrator brief. What the system is Think of it as your company's intranet with the work built in. When you sign in you land on Home : company news, the things waiting for you, and quick links. The menu on the left leads to the areas of the business you are allowed to use. Each area keeps its own records (a work order, a purchase order, a nonconformance, an expense report), and records that need a decision go to the right person as an approval. A few ideas run through everything: You see what your job needs. The menu, the pages and the buttons depend on your role and on the sites you work at. See Roles and access . Nothing is lost half-way. Forms keep what you typed while you work, and the technician screens keep working without a connection. See Getting started and Working offline and on tablets . Decisions leave a trail. Approvals, sign-offs and changes are recorded with who did them and when. The system tells you what is late. Notifications, reminders and the What is late page pull overdue work into one place. Where things are in this guide The groups below match the groups in the left-hand menu of the application. Getting started Sign in, find your way around, save your work. Roles and access Why you can or cannot see something. Offline and tablets Working without a connection; installing the app. Home and approvals Your day at a glance and what waits for your sign-off. Notifications and reminders What tells you something needs attention. Time and expenses Timesheets and expense reports. Training and performance Courses, qualifications, reviews, goals. How I like to work Text size, spacing, contrast and more. News, people, policies Announcements, the directory and the handbook. Improvements Suggest an idea and follow it to measured savings. Maintenance Assets, work orders, preventive maintenance, storerooms. Field service Agreements, dispatch and the technician's day. Production Production orders, planning, shop floor and shift log. Quality and safety Quality, CAPA, documents, safety, changes, continuity. Sales and supply Customers, quotes, purchasing, leasing. Finance Books, budgets, receivables and payables. Insight Reports and the what-is-late view. Administrator brief Setting the system up for your company. Glossary Plain-language meanings of the terms used here. If you do not have it, the button or page will not appear, or the system will say you may not. title: Getting started
text: This page takes you from the sign-in screen to a confident first day: how to get in, what the menu is telling you, where to look for what needs your attention, and how the system protects the things you type. Signing in Most companies use single sign-on : you sign in with the same company account you use for email, so there is no separate password for this system. Open the address your company gave you. The page is titled Sign in . Type your work email in Work email . Choose Continue with your company account . You go to your company's own sign-in page; sign in there as usual. You come back to the platform and land on Home . If you opened a link to a particular page before signing in, you are taken to that page instead. If the page says your company or email is not set up, or that you are not a user, ask your administrator. Signing in does not create an account; someone has to add you first. Signing in with an issued token Below the button there is a fold-out called Development sign-in with an API token . A token is a long code, beginning erp_ , that stands in for a password. Your administrator may hand one out for trials and demonstrations, or for a device that cannot use company sign-in. Paste it into API token and choose Sign in with token . Each token signs you in as one specific person, so never share yours. Tokens can be switched off for the company once single sign-on works, and single sign-on is set up per company. See Administrator brief: sign-in . If you see “Your session has ended. Sign in again.”, the system no longer recognises your sign-in. This is normal after you sign out in another window, or after your sign-in expires. Sign in again; anything you had typed into a form is waiting for you (see Saving and autosaved drafts ). The menu on the left The left-hand menu is grouped by area. On a phone or a narrow window it hides behind the Menu button at the top; press Esc or choose Close menu to put it away again. They are checked in this order: Your company has hidden it from your role. Companies can switch features on or off for each role. A hidden feature leaves the menu, and if you open its address directly you see Not available : “This part of the platform is turned off for your role.” An administrator can turn it on under Admin → Features . Your edition does not include it. The Lite edition covers the intranet, policies, expenses, customers and invoicing, suppliers and bills, the built-in books, data import and their reports. Maintenance, production, quality, safety and the rest are Standard. In Lite the menu shows only those areas, and the top-left name reads “Intranet · Lite”. See not licensed . Your role does not allow it. Each page needs a permission. For example Books needs the right to see the books, and Time shows if you are linked to an employee record or you approve or export time. See Roles and access . It is not licensed for your site. Field service appears only where field service has been licensed. You do not need to know which reason applies. Ask your administrator, and say which menu entry you expected. They can see your roles and your features. Home Home is the first page after sign-in: company news, a My work list of what is waiting for you, upcoming events and quick links. Home and approvals explains each block. Search The search box at the top of every page looks across people, policies, announcements and, where you have access, assets, documents, work orders, customers and suppliers. Click the box that says Search people, policies, assets… and type at least two characters. Press Enter . Results appear grouped by kind: People , Policies , Announcements , Assets , Documents , Work orders , Customers , Suppliers . Click a result to open it. Search shows you only what you may open. If “Nothing found” appears for something you know exists, it may be at a site you have no access to, or in a feature that is hidden from your role. On Home there is a separate box, Find a colleague , that goes straight to the people directory. The notifications bell The bell in the top bar shows how many unread notifications you have. Click it to open Notifications . See Notifications and reminders . Approvals When something needs your sign-off (an expense report, a purchase request, a document, a change), it appears under My day → Approvals and on Home. See Home and approvals . Saving and autosaved drafts You rarely need to worry about losing a half-finished form. About one second after you stop typing, the system saves what you entered on the form as a draft , on the server, under your name. title: Roles and access
text: What you can see and do in the platform is decided by your roles and by the sites where you hold them. This page explains both in plain terms, describes the roles most companies start with, and helps you read the messages you get when something is off limits. How access works A permission is one small right, such as “see work orders” or “approve timesheets”. A role is a named bundle of permissions, such as Maintenance Technician or Buyer / Purchasing. An administrator assigns roles to people. Each assignment is either company-wide or limited to one site (or a named group of sites). If you hold several roles, you have everything they give you together. The menu, the tabs on a page and the buttons all follow your permissions. A button you cannot use is usually not shown at all. The full list of permissions and which page each opens is on the Permissions table . Sites and facilities A site (the system also says “facility”) is a plant, store, building or office. Your role assignment says where it applies: Company-wide: you can use the permission at every site. People in head office roles usually have this. One site, or a group of sites: you can use the permission at those sites only. A district manager may hold a role across a group; a store manager at a single store. Site limits are enforced by the database itself, not only by the screens. If a record belongs to a site you have no role at, it will not show up in lists or in search, and opening it directly is refused. You can hold different roles at different sites; for example, technician at one plant and maintenance manager at another. Administrators assign roles and sites under the people settings. See Administrator brief: sites and people . The starter roles Every company starts with the roles below and can rename, change or add to them, so your company's list may differ. Everyone, whatever their role, can also suggest improvements, claim expenses and read published policies. Role In plain words Administrator Everything, including setup: sites, people, sign-in, features, retention, archives and imports. Maintenance Manager Runs maintenance: assets, work orders, parts and storerooms, documents, training and qualifications; approves timesheets; sees reports. Operations / Plant Manager Runs a plant: production, planning, quality and safety views, continuity, site visits, sales orders; approves timesheets; posts announcements. Production Supervisor / Planner Plans and runs production orders, shop-floor work, planning and imports; requests purchases. Operator / Requester Raises work requests, reports quality and safety problems, runs operations on the shop floor. Maintenance Technician Carries out work orders, records labor and parts, raises requests, reports quality and safety issues; sees assets, documents and stock. Field Technician Works their own service visits from a tablet: reports and customer sign-off. Service Dispatcher Plans and assigns field service visits, agreements, technicians and vehicles; prepares quotes. Quality Reviewer / Quality Manager Contains and dispositions nonconformances, owns and verifies corrective actions; the manager also controls documents. EHS / Safety Reviewer Investigates and classifies safety incidents; works on continuity plans. Trainer / Evaluator Assigns training, records attendance and shadowing, signs practical evaluations, sees training records. Property / Facilities Manager Maintenance for buildings and leased units: work orders, leasing, rent billing, site visits. District / Area Manager Oversees several sites: work requests and verification, safety, site visits and reports. Store / Site Manager Day-to-day at one site: raises requests, verifies finished work, reports problems, sees site visits. Buyer / Purchasing Suppliers and prices, purchase orders, receiving, parts catalog; sees payables. Finance Approver Approves supplier invoices, releases credit holds, reviews larger expenses, manages budgets and business cases. Accounts Payable Clerk Captures and processes supplier invoices. Billing / Accounts Receivable Invoices shipments, records payments, works the collections queue. Bookkeeper Keeps the built-in books, bank review and period lock; payables and receivables; expenses; accounting connection. Sales Representative / Sales Manager Customers, opportunities and quotes; the manager also turns quotes into orders. Payroll Administrator Sees every timesheet and produces the payroll export. HR Manager Employee records, training assignment and records, performance reviews, policies and announcements. Executive (read-only, consolidated) Reads across the company, including reports, books and business cases; changes nothing. Two things are not roles. Approving an expense report or a purchase request depends on being named in the approval route (a role at the site, a department head, or someone covering for them), not on a separate permission. And performance reviews are open to the employee and their reviewer without any permission; HR sees all. Why you may be told “no” When an action is refused, the message says why. title: Working offline and on tablets
text: Plants, basements and rural sites often have poor wifi. The platform is built so that a technician's day does not stop when the connection does. This page explains what keeps working offline, what does not, how to use the outbox, and how to put the app on a tablet or phone. What works offline Offline support covers the maintenance technician's core routine on work orders. Two things make it work: Saved copies. While you are online, the app keeps a copy on your device of your My work orders list and of each work order you open. When the connection drops, you still see those, marked “Copy saved on this device [time]: no connection right now.” The outbox. Three kinds of change can be made without a connection: labor hours, parts used , and status changes ( Start work , Put on hold , Mark complete ). Each is kept on the device, in the order you made it, until it can be sent. You can do offline You need a connection for Open a work order you have looked at before, or one on your saved list Work orders you have never opened on this device Record labor on it Creating a new work order Record a part used Looking up stock levels or parts Start, hold or complete the work Opening documents and procedures (the viewer needs a connection) Everything outside work orders, such as approvals, expenses, timesheets and reports Offline use is specific to work orders. Do not rely on it for other screens. If you work from the field service tablet screen, My day , check with your administrator how it behaves where your signal is weak; this guide only describes the work-order behaviour above. See Field service: my day . The connection bar A bar appears under the top bar whenever the state is not normal: The bar says Meaning Offline: showing copies saved on this device. N changes will be sent when you are back online. No connection. You are looking at saved copies; anything you record is waiting in the outbox. Sending N changes made offline… The connection is back and the outbox is being sent. N changes waiting to be sent. Send now You are online, but some changes have not gone yet. Choose Send now to try immediately. … N changes could not be saved. Review The server refused one or more. They stay in the outbox with the reason. No bar means you are online and nothing is waiting. Using the outbox The page Changes made offline (opened from Review in the bar, or from see all on a work order) lists everything waiting on this device. Work normally while offline. Each labor entry, part or status change you record is added to the outbox, and the work order shows “Waiting to be sent” with what is queued. When you are back online, the app sends the outbox automatically: as soon as the connection returns, and again every minute. You can also choose Send now . Open Changes made offline to check. Each row shows when it was made, what it is (for example “1.5 h labor on 2026-10-23”, “Part used × 2”, “Start work”), the work order, and its state: Waiting or Refused . For a Refused row, read the reason. If you can fix the cause (for example the work order was meanwhile cancelled or completed by someone else, or a rule was not met), choose Try again . If the change is no longer wanted, choose Discard ; you are asked to confirm, and it will not be recorded. The system sends changes in order, and a refusal of one does not stop the rest. A change is never sent twice: each carries a unique key, so if the network drops just as a change goes through, sending it again does not post it a second time. The server applies the same rules as if you had been online, so offline work never skips a check. For example, a status change that is not allowed from the work order's current status is refused with the reason. Before you sign out, make sure the outbox is empty. Signing out removes the saved copies and any unsent changes from the device, and the system warns you first. See Signing out safely . Using a tablet or phone The layout adapts to narrow screens; the menu hides behind the Menu button. Pick a larger text size and a roomier layout under How I like to work if you wear gloves or work at arm's length. Your sign-in belongs to the browser tab. If the tablet is shared, sign out at the end of the shift (after the outbox is empty). The offline copies and the outbox are kept per person on the device, so a colleague who signs in on the same tablet does not see yours. Installing the app You can install the platform as an app, so it opens in its own window from the home screen and starts even with no connection. Installing is optional; the app also works in a normal browser tab. Open the platform in your browser (Chrome or Edge on Android and desktop, Safari on iPad and iPhone) and sign in once while online. On Android or desktop, use the browser's Install app or Add to Home screen option (usually in the address bar or the browser menu). On an iPad or iPhone, choose Share and then Add to Home Screen . Open it from the new icon. It is named Ops (“Operations Platform”). The installed app keeps the page shell on the device, so it can start offline. It does not keep your data; your saved copies and outbox are the data on the device. After a software update, the new version is picked up the next time you open the app online. Common mistakes Opening a work order for the first time with no signal. It is not on the device yet. Open the day's work orders while you still have a connection. Clearing the browser's site data while changes are waiting. That removes the outbox. Send first. Using a different browser or device to look for an offline change. The outbox lives only on the device where you made the change. Ignoring a Refused row. That hours or part never reached the record. Fix or discard it. The saved copies and outbox are in the browser, so nothing needs setting up on the server. Hours reach the technician's timesheet through the work order once they are sent;

title: Home and approvals
text: Home is where each day starts: the company's news, a short list of what needs you, and quick links. Approvals is where you sign off requests that came to you. This page covers both, plus Reviews (records that must be looked at again every so often) and what to do when you are away. Your Home page Home greets you by first name and shows the date. From top to bottom: Find a colleague A search box at the top. Type a name, team or site and press Enter to open the people directory with the search applied. Company news The latest four announcements. Safety notices, events, people news and IT news have their own labels. All news and events opens the full list. Hidden if your company has switched news off for your role. My work A short list of counts, each a link: Waiting for my sign-off , Policies to read and acknowledge , My actions , My open work orders , My training to do and Overdue work orders at my sites . A coloured count means something is overdue or waiting. Items only appear if you have the matching feature and role. Documents to read Controlled documents you must read and acknowledge, with the due date or Overdue . Open each one and acknowledge it on its own page. Unsaved entries Forms you started and did not save; they are kept for you on any device. Click one to continue. See Saving and autosaved drafts . Coming up Events with a date, from the news page. Quick links The employee handbook, the people directory, and links your company added. Links to other websites open in a new tab. Below those blocks, tables list My work orders , Waiting for my sign-off and My training , as far as they apply to you. Click a row to open it. Administrators may also see a card called Worth a look with a suggestion for something to set up. Choose Show me , Not now , or Stop these suggestions . At most one is shown a week; see How I like to work . Approvals An approval is a request that needs one or more people to say yes. Approvals appear under My day → Approvals and on Home. The page title is Waiting for my sign-off . The list contains only steps you can sign right now : earlier stages are finished, you hold the role the step is addressed to (or the step is addressed to you personally, or you are covering for someone), and you are not the person who raised the request. What can arrive Label on the card What you are approving Change review, Startup authorization A change request or its start-up review. See Changes and notices . Purchase request A request to buy. The card shows the total, whether it is capital spend, who asked, and any reason it needed approval. See Purchasing . Quote pricing A quote priced below the company's limits. See Quotes and orders . Document review, Document signature A new document version. A signature asks you to enter your sign-in credential again. See Document control . FMEA review, Continuity plan approval Risk analyses and continuity plans. See Quality and Continuity . Expense reports These appear here too, and you can also decide them on the report itself. See Expenses . Deciding on an approval Open Approvals . Each request is a card. The first line says what it is and which step is yours (for example Finance review ). If you are covering for someone, it says on behalf of their name. Click the title to open the full record and check the details. Some cards link a Justification presentation . Type a comment. It is required to reject , and for some reviews it is required to approve too; then the label reads “Result of your review (required: what you checked and any conditions)”. If the card asks you to sign, enter your sign-in credential in the box provided (at least 8 characters). Choose Approve as [your role] or Reject . The card disappears and the requester is notified. Anyone who holds the role a step is addressed to, at the request's site, can approve it, or a person named personally on the step, or a delegate (below). You can never approve your own request. Separation of duties is deliberate. A very small company may allow the requester to approve their own expense report or bill if nobody else could; the record shows it as self-approved. What the statuses mean Status Meaning Pending / waiting The step is open and waiting for a decision. Approved The step was signed. When all stages are approved, the request goes ahead. Rejected A reviewer said no. The requester gets your comment and normally revises and resubmits. Cancelled The requester withdrew the request, or it was replaced by a newer revision. Away? Delegate your sign-offs At the bottom of the Approvals page, Away? Delegate your sign-offs lets someone else sign for you for a set time. Their signature records that it was on your behalf. Under Delegate to , choose a person. Set From and Until dates. Give a Reason , such as “vacation”. Choose Delegate . The table shows Scheduled before the start date, Active during, and Ended after you press End . Delegating does not give the person your permissions. It only lets them sign the steps addressed to you. A delegate cannot approve your own requests. Reviews My day → Reviews appears for people who manage records that must be looked at again every so often: FMEAs, procedures, policies, course content, suppliers, PM plans, spares lists, control limits, user access and more. It lists what is overdue or due soon. Choose the kind of record, or leave All kinds . Choose Due soon or overdue or All, with their next date . On a row, open the review. Choose No change if the record is still correct, or Changes needed and add a note about what must change. Save. The next review counts from today. If a review stays overdue, the people above you are reminded. How often each kind of record is reviewed is set by administrators. Review frequency and who is reminded are set under Admin → Reminders . See Administrator brief: reminders and retention . Seeing what is late For everything that is overdue across your work, use What is late in the Insight s

title: Assets
text: An asset is any piece of equipment you look after: a machine, a vehicle, a building space, a tool. Each has one record that collects its details, its documents, its open work, its maintenance plans and its track record. Start here when something is wrong with a machine, or when you want to know how a machine has behaved. Who can do this: anyone with access to assets can search and read records. Technicians, maintenance managers, facilities managers and district managers can change a machine's state and record meter readings. Operators, technicians and most managers can report a problem. Maintenance managers and facilities managers can edit the repair-or-replace inputs and the spare-parts list. See Roles and access . Find an asset Open Maintenance → Assets . The page is titled Equipment register . Type in Search . You can search by tag, name, model or serial number. Optionally pick a Current state to narrow the list. Click a row to open the asset. The list shows site, tag, name, location, criticality, state and the number of open work orders. If you scan the QR code on a machine with your phone or tablet, it opens the same asset page directly. What the states mean An asset is always in one operational state. The state drives the downtime figures in the reports , so keep it honest. State Meaning Running Making product or doing its job. Available Ready to use. A machine returns to this state when a work order is verified. Idle Working, but nothing is scheduled for it. Planned downtime Stopped on purpose: maintenance, changeover, a holiday. Unplanned downtime Stopped because something went wrong. This counts as a failure. Out of service Taken out of use. Change a machine's state Open the asset. Under Details , click Running , Idle , Down (unplanned) or Planned stop . The button for the current state is greyed out. The page records when the state started. You cannot set Available or Out of service with these buttons; Available comes from verifying a work order (see Work orders ). Report a problem Open the asset and find the Report a problem box. Under What is wrong? , describe the symptom in a sentence or two (at least three characters). Pick a Severity : Low, Medium, High or Critical. Tick Machine is down if it has stopped. Click Send request . This does not create a work order straight away. It sends a request to maintenance, who turn it into a work order or decline it. See Work orders: requests . What is on an asset page Details : class, manufacturer and model, serial number, criticality, in-service date, current state and how long it has been in it, plus any custom fields your company added. Change banner : if a change request affects this asset, a yellow bar names it, with a link. Temporary changes show their end date. See Changes and notices . Technical documents : approved manuals and procedures linked to the asset, with an Open link. A document with no approved version shows No approved version . See Document control . Reliability : described below. Preventive maintenance : the plans for this asset, and a place to record meter readings (only if the PM feature is on). Spare parts : the parts that belong on this machine and how many you have at the site. Repair templates : stock repair jobs with their labor hours and parts. Open work orders and Components : the child assets that belong to this one. Record a meter reading Meters (run hours, cycles, miles) trigger meter-based preventive maintenance . On the asset page, go to Preventive maintenance . Type or pick the Meter name. If the asset has a meter plan, its meter name is suggested. Enter the Reading (the total on the meter, not the change since last time). Click Record meter reading . A message tells you how much is left before the next plan is due. Reliability The Reliability card shows failures, mean time between failures (MTBF), mean time to repair (MTTR) and availability for the last 30, 90 or 365 days, with a month-by-month table. A failure is an unplanned stop. MTBF is uptime divided by failures. MTTR is unplanned downtime divided by failures. A note under the figures says where the numbers came from: from state history (best), or estimated from work orders when nobody recorded states, or no data . If state records cover only part of the period, the page tells you how much. Failure codes that repeat within 30 days appear in red. Good reliability numbers depend on people pressing the state buttons and on technicians completing work orders with a failure code. A machine with no state history still gets estimates, but they are rougher. Repair or replace For machines and vehicles (not components or spaces), the Repair or replace card compares the yearly cost of keeping the asset (maintenance plus the cost of unplanned downtime, for this asset and its components) with the equivalent yearly cost of a new one. It shows one of three verdicts: Keep , Replace or Not enough data , with the reason in a sentence, the year replacing starts to pay, and a table by year. Click Edit the inputs . Enter the Replacement cost , the Expected life (years) and the Downtime cost / h . Without a downtime cost, the downtime column shows a dash and is left out of the comparison. Click Save . This is a guide, not a decision. It uses full years only, and it leaves out resale value, energy, safety and parts availability. Use it to start the conversation about capital spending. Common mistakes Reporting a problem and expecting a work order. A request only becomes a work order when a maintenance planner accepts it. Leaving a machine in Unplanned downtime after it is fixed. Verifying the work order does this for you; if you fixed it without a work order, press Running . Entering a meter reading as the amount since last time. Enter the reading on the meter. Administrators: there is no "new asset" button on this page. Assets are loaded by import or created by your implementation team. See Importing data and Sites and people . title: Work orders
text: A work order is one job on one asset: what is wrong or what must be done, who does it, which parts and hours it used, and who checked it afterward. Every maintenance job in the system, whether a breakdown, a scheduled preventive task or a contractor visit, follows the same life cycle. Who can do this: Request a job : operators, technicians, store managers and most managers (permission "request work orders"). Create, assign, schedule, cancel, close, dispatch contractors : maintenance managers, facilities managers, district managers (permission "manage work orders"). A service dispatcher also holds it. Start work, add labor and parts, mark complete : maintenance technicians and managers (permission "execute work orders"). Verify : maintenance managers, facilities managers, district managers, store managers (permission "verify work orders"). From a request to a work order Most jobs begin as a request. Anyone can send one from an asset page ( Assets: report a problem ), and the site's public request link, if your company uses one, adds requests from outside. Requests wait in an inbox for a planner. Open Maintenance → Work orders and click Requests . (You only see this button if you can manage work orders.) Read the request: when it arrived, the site and asset, the problem, who sent it, and the severity. Down and Safety flags show in red. Critical and high requests are highlighted. Click Create work order . A short form appears with a title (taken from the problem) and a priority set from the severity. Adjust the title and priority ( 1 Emergency , 2 High , 3 Normal , 4 Low ) and click Create . The new work order opens. If the request said the machine was down, the machine is put into unplanned downtime counted from when it was reported (unless its state has changed since). If you cannot act on a request, click Decline , give a reason (duplicate, not a maintenance issue) and click Decline request . Preventive maintenance creates its own work orders. See Preventive maintenance . Field service visits get one automatically; see Field service . The work order list The list has four views: Open , Assigned to me (if you are linked to an employee record), All and Requests . Each row shows the number, site, asset, title, priority, type, status, contractor, service-level pills and due date. Overdue jobs are marked in red. What the statuses mean Status Meaning Who moves it on Planned Created, not yet scheduled. Planner can schedule, hold or cancel. A technician can start work. Scheduled Booked for a time. Same as planned. In progress Work has started. Technician can hold it or mark it complete. On hold Paused, for example waiting on a part. Technician can resume; planner can reschedule or cancel. Completed The technician says the work is done. Not yet checked. Someone with verify permission verifies it or sends it back. Verified Checked by a second person. The machine returns to service. Planner closes it. Closed Finished and filed. No further changes. Cancelled Dropped. No further changes. Open a work order and do the work Click any row to open the work order. The Next step card shows the one action available to you now, plus the description and any safety notes in a yellow box. Click Start work . The system checks that everyone assigned still holds the qualifications the machine requires, and refuses if not. Record your time with Labor (below) and parts with Parts (below) as you go. When done, fill in the form: Work done and Findings . For corrective (breakdown) jobs, What fixed it? (required) must be filled in. Click Mark work complete . At least one labor entry must exist first (or a contractor's completion). Assign people On the work order, find the People card. In Assign a technician… , pick an active employee at the site and click Assign . The system refuses if the person lacks a qualification the machine requires. You can assign until the work is completed. The new assignee is notified. Record labor While the job is In progress or On hold , use the row under Labor . Pick the Work date and enter Hours (in quarter-hours, up to 24). Click Add my hours . Hours are added under your name. You must be linked to an employee record to see the form. The card total shows hours and labor cost. Record parts While the job is In progress , use the form under Parts . Choose a part. Parts planned for this job are listed first with a star. If your site stocks the part, choose the storeroom in Taken from… . Storerooms with nothing on hand are greyed out. Enter the quantity and click Record use . Stocked parts come out of that storeroom's balance. A part that is not stocked at this site is recorded without a stock movement. To put unused parts back, click Return on the line, enter how many, and confirm. You can return until the job is closed. Kits and repair templates The Kit card helps the storeroom prepare parts in advance. A planner can apply a repair template (a stock list of parts and hours for a known job), then click Build kit from planned parts to reserve the stock. The storeroom stages the kit; the technician clicks Issue kit to this job , and later Return unused and close kit . If a kit is still reserved or staged when the job is completed or cancelled, the reservation is released automatically. Parts you do not have If planned parts exceed what has been used, a Purchasing card offers Request parts not in stock (for people who may raise purchase requests). It shows each request and order, expected dates and what has arrived. See Purchasing . Send a job to a contractor On an open work order, click Send to a contractor in the Contractor card. Optionally type a Trade to filter, choose the contractor, and set a Not to exceed ($) limit and a note. Click Dispatch . As the contractor responds, record Accepted , Declined , On site or Completed . Completing requires a note of what the contractor did. Contractors with a lapsed insurance certificate cannot be chosen. The contractor is emailed if a

title: Preventive maintenance
text: Preventive maintenance (PM) is routine work done on a schedule: lubricate every month, change filters every 500 run hours. A PM plan says what to do, on which asset, how often, and which parts it needs. When a plan comes due, the system makes a normal work order for it. Who can do this: anyone who can view work orders can see the schedule and the plans. Maintenance managers, facilities managers and district managers can create plans, pause or resume them, and generate work orders (permission "manage work orders"). Technicians and operators with meter access can record meter readings from the asset page. Where to find it Open Maintenance → PM . If you do not see it, your company has the preventive maintenance feature turned off, or you lack access to work orders. The PM schedule The page shows plans due now or in the next 60 days. Four counters across the top summarise the state of play: Overdue : plans past their due date or reading. Due now : plans inside their lead window. Due without a work order : due or overdue plans nobody has started a job for. Short of parts : plans whose parts list is not fully in stock at the site. The table lists plan code, site, asset, interval, next due, state, the current work order (if any) and a parts check ( In stock or N short ). Overdue rows are marked red. State Meaning Not due The due date or reading is still beyond the lead window. Due Inside the lead window. It is time to plan the job. Overdue The due date has passed, or the meter has reached the due reading. Paused The plan has been switched off. It does not generate work orders. Calendar plans and meter plans Calendar Due every N days. It is due from the due date minus the lead window in days. Meter reading Due every N units of a meter (run hours, cycles). It is due once the latest recorded reading reaches the due reading minus the lead amount. Readings are entered on the asset page; see Assets: record a meter reading . The plan also has a schedule basis : Count from when work is done The next due point is one interval after the work is finished. A late job pushes everything back. Keep fixed dates The next due point is one interval after the previous due point , skipping any cycle you have already passed. Dates keep their rhythm even when a job runs late. Create a plan On the PM page, click New plan . Choose the Asset . Give it a Plan code that is unique (for example PM-CNC-102-M ) and a Title . Choose the Trigger : Calendar or Meter reading . For a calendar plan, enter Every (days) . For a meter plan, enter the Meter name and Every (meter units) . Optionally set the First due date (or first due reading). If you leave it blank, the first due point is one interval from now. Choose the Schedule basis (see above). Enter Estimated hours if you know them. Under Parts list , click Add a part for each part and quantity the job uses. Click Create plan . The plan opens. Use the same meter name every time (for example always run_hours ). The asset page suggests the meter names already in use. Generate work orders Work orders from PM are made when you ask for them, not automatically in the background. On the PM page, click Generate due work orders . A green message lists what was created (work order number and plan), and which plans were skipped because they already have an open work order. Generation makes one work order per due plan and never a duplicate. Each is a preventive work order titled "PM: ..." with the plan's parts planned on it. If the parts are stocked at the site, the stock is reserved in a kit so it is waiting when work starts. Technicians then work the job as usual. The plan only moves forward when its work order is verified , not when it is completed. If nobody verifies, the plan stays due and, once the job is closed, will be due again. See Work orders: verify . A plan's page Click a plan to see its schedule: trigger and basis, next due, lead window, last done (date and reading), estimated time and procedure document. Beside it is the parts list with On hand at site and a Short flag. Below is the history of work orders from the plan, each marked On time or Late . Pause or resume a plan Open the plan. Type a reason in the box (at least five characters, for example "asset idle until Q1"). Click Pause plan (or Resume plan when it is paused). The reason is kept in the audit trail. Common mistakes Waiting for work orders to appear on their own. Press Generate due work orders regularly, or rely on the reminder (below). Forgetting to enter meter readings. A meter plan with no reading yet never becomes due. Completing the work order but never verifying it, so the plan does not advance. Planning a part that is not stocked at the site. The plan shows not stocked , and the job's kit is not built. Administrators: a daily reminder, "PM plans due without a work order", goes to maintenance planners at the site when a plan is inside its lead window and has no open work order. You can change or turn it off under Reminders and retention . The whole PM area can be hidden under Features and editions .

title: Storerooms
text: Storerooms hold your spare parts. Every change to a quantity, whether a receipt, an issue to a work order, a return, a transfer, an adjustment or a count, is written to a ledger, so you can always see how a balance came about. This page shows stock by storeroom and is where you receive, adjust, count and track lots. Who can do this: anyone with stock access (technicians, buyers, managers) can view stock, the ledger, lots and kits. Maintenance managers and others with "manage inventory" can receive parts, post adjustments, set reorder levels, run counts, put lots on hold and map barcodes. Issuing parts to a work order only needs the right to work on that job. Changing a part's tracking or units needs "manage parts" (maintenance managers and buyers). Open Maintenance → Storerooms . There are four tabs: Stock , Lots , Kits and Cycle counts . For barcode work on a tablet see Scan station . Stock on hand Four counters sit at the top: Stocked lines , At or below reorder point , Out of stock and Stock value (at average cost). Below, search by part number or description, or tick Only at or below reorder point . A row shows storeroom, part, bin, on-hand quantity, reorder level and last movement, with an Out or Reorder badge where needed. See how a balance came about Click a stock row. A panel opens for that part at that storeroom. Read the movements: when, type, quantity (+ or -), balance after, reference (work order, packing slip or reason) and who did it. Receive parts Use this for stock arriving without going through a purchase order. If you have a purchase order, receive against it so the order stays accurate; see Purchasing or the scan station . On the Stock tab, scroll to Receive parts . Choose the Storeroom and the Part . Enter the Quantity . Optionally add Unit cost (USD) and a Packing slip / PO reference. If the part is tracked, enter the lot (with an expiry date if it has one) or list the serial numbers, one per line. The page shows "N of M serial numbers" so you can check the count. Click Receive . A green message gives the new balance. You can split a delivery across lots with Split into another lot . The unit cost feeds the part's average cost. Issue parts Parts leave a storeroom in one of three ways: A technician records Record use on a work order and chooses the storeroom. See Work orders: record parts . A storeroom clerk issues a prepared kit to the job. See Kits . The Kits tab lists open kits needed by date, with any shortage flagged. The scan station issues by scanning to a work order or a job reference. Stock cannot go below zero. If a tracked part has several lots, the first to expire is used unless someone chooses another; lots on hold or past expiry are never issued. Adjust a balance Click the stock row to open the part panel. Under Adjust , enter Change (+ or -) and a Reason of at least five characters, such as "damaged in storage". For a tracked part, enter the lot or serial. It is required when adding, and optional when removing (blank means the first to expire). Click Post adjustment . For finding a difference on the shelf, a count is better than an adjustment: it records what you found and posts the difference for you. Reorder levels Open the part panel. Under Reorder settings , set the Reorder point and Reorder quantity . Click Save . A part at or below its reorder point is flagged Reorder and counted in the top counters. Buyers then raise a purchase request; see Purchasing . Units of measure A part is stocked and counted in one unit, shown in the Units section of the part panel. If it is bought in packs, boxes, cases or drums, someone with part-management rights can add a unit ("1 BOX = 100 EA"), so purchasing and receiving convert for you. A unit that a supplier is priced in cannot be removed. Counting stock Open the Cycle counts tab. It lists counts with storeroom, status, how many lines are counted, and when opened and posted. Choose a Storeroom to count… and click Start a count . A count sheet opens listing every part there, with bin and the expected quantity as of that moment. Count the shelf. Enter each Counted quantity. Click Save counts to keep your progress. If you find a tracked lot that is not on the sheet, use Found a lot that is not on the sheet to add it. When every line is counted, click Post count . A green message lists the differences, or "No variances." If stock moved while you counted, the page stops and says so. Click Post against current quantities to accept the moves and post the differences against today's numbers. Count status Meaning Open Still being counted. Counts can be saved and continued. Posted Differences have been written to the ledger. The sheet is read-only. A count started on the scan station is blind : expected quantities are hidden until it is posted, so the counter is not nudged toward the book figure. Lots and serial numbers A part can be tracked by lot (a batch, often with an expiry date) or by serial number (one unit each). The Lots tab lists tracked stock. Search by lot, serial, supplier lot or part, or use the filter: In stock , Expired or expiring within 30 days , or On hold . Lot status Meaning Available Can be issued or shipped. Expired Past its expiry date. Never issued or shipped. On hold Blocked, with a reason. Never issued or shipped. Scrapped Written off. Switch tracking on for a part Open the part panel from the Stock tab. Under Lot and serial tracking , choose By lot or By serial number . Optionally set a Shelf life in days, which fills in expiry dates on receipt. If stock is already on hand, enter a lot number (and expiry) for each storeroom's quantity so it can be put into a lot now. Click Save . To track by serial number, count the stock out to zero first (or track by lot). The page warns you if there is stock on hand. A lot's page Click a lot to see where it is, what it was made from, where it went (production orders, customer shipments, work orders) and every movement. Print label makes a barcode

title: Scan station
text: The scan station is a touch-friendly screen for the storeroom. You receive deliveries, issue parts to jobs and count shelves by scanning barcodes instead of typing. It posts exactly the same ledger entries as the typed screens on Storerooms ; it is simply faster and makes fewer mistakes. Who can do this: everyone with stock access can open the station and use Look up and Labels . Receive , Issue , Count and Barcodes need the "manage inventory" right (maintenance managers). Someone who can receive purchase orders (buyers) also sees Receive . Technicians with only view access see just the lookup and label tabs. What you need A tablet or computer with a browser, signed in to the system, with a connection. The station does not work offline. A USB or Bluetooth scanner that acts like a keyboard, which needs no setup. Or use the tablet's camera where the browser supports it. Or type the code and press Enter . Open Maintenance → Scan station . Across the top are the modes. A coloured banner under them confirms each scan, with a beep for success or failure. A wrong scan is refused with the reason, and nothing is posted. What the codes mean Whatever is scanned is looked up and recognised as one of these: Scan What it is L:CODE A storeroom location. The L: prefix is reserved for our location labels. LOT:PARTNUMBER:LOTNUMBER A lot or serial number. The LOT: prefix is reserved for our lot labels. A plain part number A part. Checked first. A supplier's UPC, EAN, carton or supplier code A part, if someone has mapped that code to it (see Barcodes ). A purchase order number A purchase order, if you may receive for that site. A work order number A work order, if you may view it. A plain location code A location. This works as a fallback when there is no L: prefix. The prefixes exist so a location code and a part number can never be mistaken for each other. Anything unrecognised is refused with "is not a part, location, lot, purchase order or work order here". Receive Choose the Receive tab. Scan the purchase order. The station shows the order's lines with ordered, received and to-come quantities. If there is no order, skip this step: the screen says "none (receiving without an order)". If there is no order, scan the shelf location . With an order, each line already knows its storeroom. Scan the part. Scanning the same part again adds to the quantity (one scan adds the part's "quantity per scan", normally 1). With an order, a part that is not an open line is refused. Check the quantity, using the minus and plus buttons if needed. For a lot- or serial-tracked part, enter the lot or serial number and, if it has one, the expiry date. Press Receive . The banner says what was received and how many lines are still open. With an order, the receipt is posted against it; without, it is a plain receipt with the reference "Scan receipt". Quantities are limited to what is still to come on the line. Press Clear order to start again. Issue Choose the Issue tab. Scan the storeroom location you are taking from. Scan the work order , or type a job, cost centre or line in Job, cost centre or line if there is no work order. Scan the part. The banner shows how many are on hand at that location, and turns red if none are. Check the quantity, then press Issue . Issuing to a work order records the part on that job, with labor and cost, the same as Record use on the work order. Issuing to a reference is a plain stock issue. The station does not issue lot- or serial-tracked parts: it tells you to issue those from the work order or the storeroom screen, where the lot is chosen. Count Choose the Count tab. The Due for counting table lists storerooms with parts due by schedule. Either press Count these (or Continue ) beside a storeroom, or scan a shelf location to start or continue a count there. Scan each part. Enter what is on the shelf with the plus and minus buttons or by typing. For a tracked part, choose the lot or serial number. Press Save count . The list Still to count shrinks as you go. When it is empty, press Finish and post . If you must stop, press Leave it open and continue later. Counts from the station are blind : the screen does not show the expected quantity, so you count what you see. When posted, the banner lists any differences ("Posted. 2 differences: ...") or says everything matched. If stock moved during the count, a red button appears: Stock moved during the count: post against current quantities . The count schedule A part at a storeroom can be given a count interval in days (up to three years). It becomes due when it has never been counted, or the last count was longer ago than the interval. The station groups the due parts by storeroom. "Count these" opens a count containing only what is due. If nothing is listed, no part has an interval set. The station says to set it "on the storeroom screen", but the storeroom screen in this version does not show a count interval field. Ask your administrator how the intervals are loaded in your company. Look up Scan anything on the Look up tab to see what it is. For a part you get description, unit, whether it is tracked, and where it is on hand. For a location, its code and name (and an Inactive badge if closed). For a lot, its status and expiry. For an order or work order, its status and open lines. Labels Open the Labels tab. Choose Label for Storeroom locations or Parts . Tick the rows you want. Press Print N labels . A PDF opens. Print it on Avery 5160 label sheets (30 per page, three across). Location labels carry the L: code; part labels carry the plain part number. Lot and serial labels are printed from the lot's own page (see Storerooms: a lot's page ). A code that cannot be printed as a barcode (letters, digits and punctuation only, up to 48 characters) is refused with a message. Barcodes Suppliers' cartons often have their own barcode. Map it once and it scans as your part. Open the Barcodes tab and choose a Part . Enter the Code (3 to 60 characters), t

title: Field service
text: Field service is for companies whose business is maintaining other people's equipment on a schedule. A customer signs a service agreement covering some equipment. The system generates visits on the agreed frequency. A coordinator (the dispatcher) assigns each visit to a technician. The technician does the work on a tablet (see Field service: My day ), and the visit is billed. Field service is licensed per site . If your site does not have the field service licence, the menu is hidden and the pages refuse to open. Ask your administrator; see the box at the end. Who can do this: a service dispatcher (permission "manage field service") can create call-outs and agreements, assign and unassign visits, send the day to a technician, cancel visits, and manage technicians, trucks and settings. Field technicians have "execute field service" and use My day. Managing billing and creating invoices needs receivables authority ("view receivables" to see the Billing tab and "manage receivables" to create invoices). Making quotes needs the right to quote (service dispatchers and sales representatives). Open Field service → Field service . The tabs are Dispatch , Visits , Agreements , Technicians, trucks and tools , Billing and Settings . Billing shows only to people with receivables access, and Settings only to dispatch managers. A Performance report button at the top opens the service report; see Reports . Agreements An agreement is a contract with one customer for one servicing site. It lists the units it covers and how often each is serviced. On the Agreements tab, click New agreement . Choose the Customer and Servicing site . Set Starts and (optionally) Ends . Choose Billing : Per visit (enter a fee per visit) or Flat monthly (enter a monthly fee). Optionally set the Response time for call-outs (hours) , tick Parts are included in the fee and Renews automatically , and add Terms . Click Save draft . On the agreement, under Add a covered unit , choose the equipment, name the service (for example "Quarterly PM"), set Every N weeks, months or years, the First due date, estimated minutes, any skill needed, a checklist (one item per line) and, if different, a fee for this unit. Click Add . Click Activate (generates the visits) . At least one unit must be covered. Equipment must already belong to the customer. Visits are created ahead of time (30 days by default, see Settings ), one per plan and date. If a plan fell behind, you get one overdue visit, not a pile. Agreement status Meaning Draft Being set up. No visits yet. Active Visits are being generated. Suspended Paused with a reason. Activate resumes it. Ended Finished normally, with a reason. Cancelled Cancelled, with a reason. Suspend , End and Cancel each need a reason of at least three characters. To stop covering one unit use Remove beside it, and Restore to bring it back. Call-outs A call-out is an unscheduled visit for a breakdown. On the Visits tab, click New call-out . Choose the Customer , then the Equipment (add new equipment to the customer first). Set Priority , Needed by , Minutes and any Skill needed . Describe What is wrong and add notes. Click Create call-out . The visit appears under To schedule on the dispatch board with a Call-out tag. Visits and their statuses The Visits tab lists visits (filter Open visits , Overdue or All ). Click one to open it. Status Meaning To schedule Exists, not yet assigned. Scheduled Assigned to a technician on a day. The technician has been told. Dispatched The day has been sent to the technician. On site The technician started the visit. Done The service report was submitted. Cancelled Cancelled with a reason. An Overdue tag appears when the due date has passed. To cancel a visit that is not yet started, type a reason (at least three characters) and click Cancel visit . The dispatch board The Dispatch tab shows one day. Use the arrows, the date or Today to change day. There is one card per technician, showing: How full the day is as a percentage (green, amber over 85%, red if overbooked), or why they are not working (for example time off). Their skills, and minutes on site plus minutes driving against the day's capacity. Their stops: arrival time, visit, customer and site, and drive minutes. Under the cards, To schedule lists visits with no technician in the next week, with customer, what, due date, minutes and skill. Assign a visit In To schedule , click Assign… on a visit. A panel ranks the technicians. For each you see Can take it or the reasons they cannot (missing skill, not working that day, time off, too many booked hours), Extra drive , visits already that day and minutes free afterward. Click Assign beside a technician who can take it. Assigning creates the visit's work order , assigns the technician to it and notifies them. The system picks a start time: after the technician's previous stop plus drive time, or the start of their day. It refuses a visit that would run past the end of the day. To undo, click Unassign on the stop; it goes back to To schedule . Send the day When a technician's day is right, click Send the day to NAME . All their scheduled visits for that day change to Dispatched . How drive time is estimated The system does not use a maps service. Drive time is the straight-line distance between stops multiplied by a road factor , divided by an average speed . Both are typed in Settings (the note above the board shows the current values). A stop with a star after the minutes is an estimate because a site or technician has no map coordinates; the system then assumes 20 minutes. Treat all drive times as a guide for ranking people, not a promise to the customer. Technicians, trucks and tools Technicians : shows name, skills, working hours, truck and visits today. A dispatcher turns an employee into a technician by choosing them, entering Skills (comma separated) and optional home latitude and longitude, and clicking Save technician . Trucks : add a vehicle with a tag, name

title: Field service: My day
text: My day is the screen a field technician uses on a tablet in the truck and at the customer's site. It shows your stops for the day in order, with the time to arrive, the customer's address, access notes and the equipment. When you start a visit you fill in the service report. Submitting it completes the job and sends it for billing. Who can do this: field technicians (permission "execute field service"). You must also be set up as a technician by your dispatcher, or the page says "You are not set up as a technician. Ask your dispatcher." Field service must be licensed for your site. Open Field service → My day . Your dispatcher's side of this is described in Field service . Your route Use the arrows or the date box to move between days. Each stop is a card showing: The arrival time and customer, and the status of the stop (scheduled, dispatched, in progress or completed). What the job is and the equipment tag and name. The site and address, drive time from the previous stop (marked "estimate" if the system could not use map coordinates), and the expected minutes on site. Access notes in a yellow box, for example where to park or who to ask for. The make, model and serial number of the equipment. "Nothing is scheduled for you on this day" means you have no visits assigned. You are told in the app when a visit is assigned to you. Start a visit Find the stop. Its button says Start the visit while it is scheduled or dispatched. Tap Start the visit when you arrive. The report form opens and the stop turns to in progress . Once a visit is in progress, the button on the card reads Service report (or Hide the report when the form is open). A finished stop shows View report . Fill in the service report Work from the top of the form to the bottom. Everything is large enough to use with a finger. Checklist. If the visit has a checklist, tap OK , Issue or N/A for every item. For an Issue , type what is wrong. You must answer every item before you can submit. Readings. Tap Add a reading for measurements such as amps or pressure. Give the name, the value and the unit. Work performed. Describe what you did (at least five characters). This is required. Findings. Anything you noticed. Hours on site. Enter hours in quarter-hour steps. This is required and must be more than zero and no more than 24. The problem is fixed. On a call-out, tick this when you solved it. Parts used (from the truck). Tap Add a part , choose the part and quantity. Parts come off your truck's stock, and cannot go below zero. Other work the customer needs. Tap Add a recommended repair for anything else you found. Describe it, choose Now , Soon or When convenient , and enter a price if you know it. Each becomes a line on a draft quote that the office can send. Customer sign-off. If the customer is there, leave The customer is here to sign ticked, type their name and have them sign in the box. If they are not, untick it and say why (not on site, refused, locked out). Tap Submit report . Tap Save draft at any point. It keeps your report on the server so you can come back to it. When you reopen a saved draft, the fields start empty; the page tells you a draft was saved at a given time, so fill it in again before you submit. About the signature If the customer is present, both a typed name (at least two characters) and a drawn signature are required. If they are not, a short reason is required instead. The signature image is stored with the report and shown to the office as View signature . What happens when you submit Your hours are recorded as labor on the visit's work order. Your parts are taken off your truck's stock and recorded on the work order. Checklist items marked Issue are added to the findings. The work order is marked completed. A second person with verify rights checks it later, as for any work order . The visit becomes Done and the report is marked for billing: ready to invoice, or covered by the customer's agreement. If you listed recommended repairs, the dispatchers are notified to quote them. After submitting you cannot change the report. Tell your dispatcher if something is wrong. What the stop statuses mean Status shown Meaning scheduled Assigned to you for this day. dispatched Your dispatcher has sent the day. It behaves the same as scheduled. in progress You started it. The report can be filled in. completed The report is submitted. Tools and truck stock Tools are checked out and returned by the dispatcher or by you on the dispatcher's Technicians, trucks and tools tab if you have access. A tool that is overdue for calibration cannot be checked out. See Field service: technicians, trucks and tools . Common mistakes Submitting without answering every checklist item or without hours. The form tells you what is missing. Choosing a part you did not carry. The system takes it from your truck's stock and refuses if the truck does not have enough. Forgetting that the customer must sign, or that a reason is needed when they do not. Leaving a report open overnight with only a draft saved. A draft does not complete the visit. Administrators: to use this page a person needs the Field Technician role and a technician profile (skills, working hours, optional truck and home coordinates), and the site needs the field service licence. See Field service , Features and editions and Offline and tablets . The service report page itself does not queue work when you are offline; you need a connection to start a visit and to submit.

title: Production orders
text: A production order is an instruction to make a stated quantity of one part at one site, by a due date. It follows the part's released product revision: the list of materials per unit and the routing (the ordered operations, each at a work center). This page covers the Production menu's Orders , Products and Work centers tabs. Running the work on the floor is covered in Shop floor and shift log . Who can do this: See orders, products and work centers : anyone with "view production", such as operators, production supervisors, plant managers, quality staff and sales. Create and release orders, edit and release product revisions, add work centers, cancel, complete short, close : production supervisors/planners and plant managers (permission "manage production"). Issue materials, receive finished goods, start and stop runs : operators and production supervisors (permission "execute production"), for their own site. Request what is short : needs the purchasing request permission as well. Production is part of the Standard edition and can be switched off per company, so you may not see these pages. See the administrator note at the end. Where to find it Open Production → Production orders . Four tabs run across the top: Orders , Shop floor , Products and Work centers . The three tiles on the Orders tab show open orders, late orders and orders in progress. Tick Only open and completed to hide closed and cancelled orders. Late orders are marked in red. What the statuses mean Status Meaning What moves it on Planned The order exists but has no materials or operations yet. Quantity can still change. A manager releases it, or cancels it. Released Materials and operations were copied from the current released revision. The floor can see it. The first run started on the floor makes it In progress. A manager can still cancel it if no material has been issued. In progress At least one run has started. Receiving the full quantity completes it. A manager can complete it short. Completed The full quantity was received, or the order was completed short with a reason. A manager closes it. Closed Finished and filed. No further changes. — Cancelled Dropped, with a reason. No further changes. — A Late tag appears beside any planned, released or in-progress order whose due date has passed. Create an order On the Orders tab, click New production order . Choose Part to make… . Only parts with a released revision are offered, and the revision number is shown. Choose the Site , enter the Quantity , and optionally a due date. Choose Finished goods to… , the storeroom at that site where the made parts will go. You can leave it for later, but you cannot receive goods until it is set. Click Create . The order opens as Planned . If the part has no released revision, the order is refused. Start with the Products tab (below). Orders can also come from the plan: the Planned production table on the Planning page has a "create order" link for each part and month. Release it to the floor Open the planned order and click Release to the floor . The system copies the materials and operations from the part's current released revision. A message tells you whether all materials are covered, or lists the parts that are short. The order keeps the revision it was released with, even if a newer revision is released later. If the routing uses a work center at a different site, release is refused; make the order at that site instead. Materials: what is short, issuing, and making sub-assemblies The Materials table shows, for each part, the quantity required, issued so far, available at the site, and any shortage. Rows with a shortage are highlighted. A purchased part is short : click Request what is short . A purchase request is drafted for the shortfall, less what is already on order or already requested. It opens for you to review. See Purchasing . A part marked "made in house" is short : managers see a Make link beside the shortfall. It creates a new production order for the missing quantity, with the same due date. In the Materials table, enter the quantity under Issue now for each line. Choose the storeroom if more than one holds stock. For lot-tracked parts, choose the lot. Or click Fill remaining to propose the quantity still needed, up to what the first storeroom holds. Click Issue materials . The stock moves out of the storeroom onto the order and appears in Stock movements at the bottom of the page. Once some goods are finished, the Variance column shows how actual usage compares with the standard quantity. Operations and the shop-floor record The Operations table lists each step in order: work center, what is done, quantity received from the previous step, good, scrap and reworked counts, and minutes actual against standard. A linked work instruction opens in the document viewer (see Document control ). An operation cannot start until the previous one is finished. Operators normally start work from the Shop floor tab. If you are linked to an employee record and allowed to run production, a Start button also appears on the order itself and takes you to the right work center. The Shop-floor record lists every run with times, operator, machine, quantities and notes. For a run that scrapped parts, people who may report quality problems see Raise NCR , which opens a nonconformance already linked to the run (see Quality ). Receive finished goods When the last operation has reported good units that are not yet received, a Receive finished goods card appears. Enter the Quantity to receive . It cannot exceed what the last operation reported and you have not yet received. If the part is serial-tracked, enter the serial numbers. If it is lot-tracked, the lot is the order number. Click Receive . The goods go into the finished-goods storeroom at the standard material cost shown on the card. When the whole quantity has been received, the order becomes Completed by itself. title: Planning
text: The Planning page turns customer forecasts and firm sales orders into two answers. First, how loaded each work center will be, month by month, against the hours it can really deliver. Second, which purchased materials you will be short of, and the date by which you must order them. You can try "what if" scenarios without changing anything, and you can turn the plan into purchase requests and production orders with one click. Who can do this: See the plan and forecasts : plant managers, production supervisors/planners, buyers, sales staff and executives (permission "view planning"). Create scenarios, draft purchase requests, create production orders, activate forecasts, edit calendars and consumption rates : plant managers and production supervisors/planners (permission "manage planning"). Creating orders also needs the production manage permission; drafting a purchase request needs the purchasing request permission. Open Production → Planning . Pick the site in the box at the top right (only plant sites are listed). Tabs: Plan , Forecasts , and, for managers, Calendars and Consumables . Reading the Plan tab Choose a Horizon of 3, 6, 9 or 12 months. The tiles at the top summarise the plan: Peak load The busiest work center in the busiest month, as a percentage of its capacity. Work-center months over How many work center and month combinations need more than 100 percent of capacity. Materials short How many purchased parts you will not have enough of in the horizon. Operator shortfall Shown only when work centers require qualifications. Counts work-center months where there are not enough qualified people. Firm share of demand How much of the demand is firm sales orders rather than forecast. Work-center load Each cell shows a percentage and "hours needed / hours available". The colour shows how tight it is. Colour Load Meaning Green 85 percent or less Comfortable. Amber Over 85 up to 100 percent Tight. Little room for breakdowns or rush orders. Red Over 100 percent Overloaded. The plan cannot be met without more capacity or less demand. Hover over a cell to see the pieces: hours from open production orders, firm orders, forecast, and the capacity after preventive maintenance. A line under the work center name shows its hours per week, number of machines or crews, and availability. Load is open production orders plus planned production (firm and forecast), run through each part's released routing. Capacity is the calendar hours times the machines or crews, times the availability the machines have actually demonstrated (from their recorded state), less preventive maintenance hours projected from the machines' calendar PM plans. In each month, for a customer and part, the larger of the forecast and the firm orders counts, so firm orders above the forecast are never lost. Qualified operators If work centers require qualifications, a second table shows, per month, either "covered" or "N h short" of qualified people. A work center that depends on one person (or nobody) gets a tag. A list below names people whose qualification expires within the horizon and how many qualified people the work center will then have. People are shared: someone qualified on two work centers is counted once. See Training and performance . Materials The table lists each purchased part the plan needs, with the quantity available now, needed, on order, short, already requested, the date it is needed by, and the Order by date. A red past tag means the order-by date has already gone by. The For column says whether the demand comes from production, consumption (coolant, inserts, chemicals) or preventive maintenance parts. Turning the plan into action These buttons appear only for the plan "as planned", never when a scenario is selected, and only if you have the permissions above. To buy what is short, click Draft a purchase request for N short materials above the Materials table. A draft request opens for you to review and submit for approval. The shortfalls already requested or on order are not repeated. See Purchasing . To make something, find the part and month in the Planned production table and click create order . A planned production order is created. Release it when you are ready. See Production orders . Try a scenario A scenario changes the plan on screen without changing any real data. Use it to ask "what if demand rises 15 percent" or "what if we add a second shift on the lathes". Click New scenario . Give it a name, for example "Second shift on lathes". Enter a Forecast change in percent (for example 15 or -10). Optionally pick a work center and enter extra hours per week and extra machines or crews. Click Save and show . The tiles now show the new peak load and note what it was before. Choose As planned (no scenario) in the scenario box to go back to the real plan. Assumptions the plan made If the plan had to guess, for example a work center without a calendar, it lists the guesses under Assumptions this plan had to make . Read this before relying on the numbers. Forecasts The Forecasts tab lists the customer forecasts for the site: customer, version, status, months covered, total quantity, date received and source. Click one to see the quantities per part and month. Each cell shows the change from the version before it, and the firm sales-order quantity in that month. A red "firm" figure means firm orders already exceed the forecast. Status Meaning Draft Imported but not yet used by the plan. Active The version the plan uses for that customer. Superseded An earlier version, replaced when a newer one was activated. Kept for history. Import the customer's forecast (see the administrator note). Open the new draft and compare it with the previous version. Managers click Use this version in the plan .
